demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: For trauma type 'unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one', the body-focused appraisals 'I can no longer trust my own body' and 'I feel ashamed of what happened to my body' are hard to reconcile clinically unless the patient also directly experienced major bodily violation/injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

The memory items imply vivid sensory reliving of the traumatic event ('hear things ... heard during the frightening event') and fragmented visual snapshots, which can occur in PTSD, but here they are not well matched to the selected appraisals: the profile centers on bodily shame/unreliability rather than grief/death-related meanings of the event.

'Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study' is not impossible, but in this profile it appears weakly integrated: there are no trigger or threat items tying work contexts to the trauma, and the formulation does not include trigger/threat pathways. The coping profile otherwise concerns sleep delay and undereating, so work avoidance feels insufficiently anchored.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, body-focused shame is clinically hard to reconcile unless there was also direct bodily violation, injury, or assault. The rest of the profile centers grief-related loss, meaning, and intrusive memory phenomena, so this item appears inconsistent with the trauma type and with the other selected items.

vignette:
Leilani, a 46-year-old forensic analyst, remembers the day her younger sister, Kiana, died with a chilling, fragmented clarity. It was a Tuesday morning, a day like any other, until the sudden, guttural sound from the kitchen. Leilani had been in the living room, and the memory of Kiana's sharp gasp, a sound unlike anything she had ever heard, still reverberates in her mind, sometimes startlingly loud, as if it just happened. When Leilani rushed in, she found Kiana on the floor, her eyes wide and unseeing. That image-Kiana's face, pale and still against the patterned kitchen tiles-is burned into Leilani's memory, a snapshot she revisits unwillingly, repeatedly. The paramedics' urgent voices and the sterile hiss of the oxygen tank are other sounds that sometimes replay in her head, leaving her breathless.

In the months that followed, these fragments of memory would ambush Leilani without warning. When the memory returns, she feels so overwhelmed by emotion - a crushing wave of grief, shock, and helplessness - that she has to stop whatever she is doing. If she is driving, she pulls over. If she is trying to talk to her husband, her words catch in her throat. This overwhelming sensation makes her dread the quiet moments, the times when her mind is free to wander. She started staying up until very late, scrolling aimlessly through her phone or watching television until the early hours, anything to delay the moment she had to turn out the lights and face the silence of her thoughts. Sleep offered no escape; nightmares often brought her back to that kitchen floor.

Her work as a forensic analyst, once a source of quiet satisfaction and purpose, became a relentless minefield. The meticulous examination of evidence, often related to unexpected deaths or accidents, began to feel unbearable. The sterile lighting of the lab, the precise movements required, even the faint metallic scent of certain samples, would sometimes trigger a rush of Kiana's final moments. She found herself delaying going to work, hitting snooze repeatedly, or finding excuses to call in sick. When she did make it in, she would procrastinate opening new case files, leaving them untouched for days, the stack on her desk growing taller. She had come to believe that her life had been utterly destroyed by the trauma, that the vibrant, hopeful person she once was had ceased to exist the moment Kiana took her last breath. What was the point of methodically analyzing evidence when life itself felt so arbitrary and cruel?

This pervasive sense of meaninglessness extended beyond her job. Leilani found herself losing interest in activities she once cherished with her husband, like their evening walks or cooking together. She had lost her faith in people, in life's inherent fairness, and even in any higher power that might oversee such senseless suffering. Food, too, became a struggle. The knot of anxiety and grief in her stomach made eating unappealing, and she often found herself avoiding meals or restricting what she ate, almost as if denying her body sustenance was a way to exert control over a life that felt utterly out of control. The weight loss was noticeable, and her husband's concerned glances were becoming more frequent.

The growing backlog of cases at work, coupled with a formal warning from her supervisor about her declining performance, finally prompted Leilani to seek help. She felt perpetually exhausted, her body aching from lack of sleep and nourishment, and her mind a constant battlefield of intrusive images and sounds. What frightened her most was the certainty that her life, as she knew it, was irrevocably broken, and she desperately wanted to understand if there was any way to piece together the fragments of herself that remained.
